metadata.description:
Case name: Slack v. McDaniel

Opinion filed: 2000-04-26

Docket No.: 98-6322

Citations:
• 146 L. Ed. 2d 542
• 120 S. Ct. 1595
• 529 U.S. 473
• 2000 U.S. LEXIS 3000

Case holding summaries:
• “Where a plain procedural bar is present and the district court is correct to invoke it to dispose of the case, a reasonable jurist could not conclude . . . that the district court erred in dismissing the petition.”
• “AEDPA’s present provisions . . . incorporate earlier habeas corpus principles”
• "We join with every other court to consider the question, and hold that a habeas petition filed after a previous petition has been dismissed on exhaustion grounds is not a `second or successive' petition"
• "Those prisoners who . . . submit mixed petitions nevertheless are entitled to resubmit a petition with only exhausted claims or to exhaust the remainder of their claims"
• refusing to apply rules governing second or successive petitions to a petitioner whose prior habeas petition had been dismissed for failure to exhaust
• merits of claim and procedural bar must be debatable to justify COA
• using pre-AEDPA law to interpret AEDPA's provision governing "second or successive habeas applications"
• dealing with § 2254 motion and stating that the court of appeals should have treated the notice of appeal as an application for a COA
• “W here a plain procedural bar is present and the district court is correct to invoke it to dispose of the case, a reasonable jurist could not conclude either that the district court erred in dismissing the petition or that the petitioner should be allowed to proceed further.”
• noting Congress' substitution of "`constitutional'" for "`federal'" in the standard for obtaining a certificate of probable cause the COA's predecessor without saying if the change is meaningful
• explaining how to satisfy this showing
• holding that a certificate of appealability should -2- issue only if the petitioner “demonstrate[s] that reasonable jurists would find the district court’s assessment of the constitutional claims debatable or wrong”
• “[T]he Court of Appeals should have treated the notice of appeal as an application for a COA.”
• "A petition filed after a mixed petition has been dismissed under Rose v. Lundy before the district court adjudicated any claims is to be treated as `any other first petition' and is not a second or successive petition."
• first quoting 28 U.S.C. § 2253(c), then quoting Barefoot v. Estelle, 463 U.S. 880, 893 n.4 (1983)
• a substantial showing of the denial of a constitutional right includes a showing that reasonable jurists could debate whether the petition should have been resolved in a different manner or that the issues presented were adequate to deserve encouragement to proceed further
• “a habeas petition which is filed after an initial petition was dismissed without adjudication on the merits for failure to exhaust state remedies is not a ‘second or successive’ petition”
• holding that to obtain COA, “petitioner must demonstrate that reasonable jurists would find the district court’s assessment of the constitutional claims debatable or wrong”
• holding that the dismissal of a petitioner’s claims under 28 U.S.C. § 2254, for failure to exhaust his state remedies, should not render a subsequent petition “second or successive”

• holding that "§ 2253 applies to appellate proceedings initiated post-AEDPA[,]" even when the underlying habeas proceeding was initiated a district court pre-AEDPA
• stating that "‘second or successive peti- tion’ is a term of art given substance in our prior habeas corpus cases" and that the Court did not "suggest the definition of second or succes- sive would be different under AEDPA"
• “Where a plain procedural bar is present and the district court is correct to invoke it to dispose of the case, a reasonable jurist could not conclude . . . that the district court erred in dismissing the petition . . . .”
• noting that pre-AEDPA law, including the abuse of the writ doctrine, should be used in interpreting the meaning of the term of art "second or successive" in AEDPA
• a COA should be granted where the applicant has made "a substantial showing of the denial of a constitutional right," i.e., when "reasonable jurists would find the district court's assessment of the constitutional claims debatable or wrong"
• holding that when a habeas petitioner seeks to initiate an appeal of the dismissal of his petition after AEDPA's effective date, the right to appeal is governed by the COA requirements found in § 2253(c
• notwithstanding inclusion of new claims, habeas petition filed after initial petition was dismissed without prejudice for failure to exhaust remedies is not a "second or successive" petition

• holding that second habeas petition raising claims dismissed in previous “mixed” petition was not second or successive
• construing 28 U.S.C. § 2253(c)
• requiring a "substantial showing of the denial of a constitutional right"
• certificates of appealability may issue if “the prisoner shows, at least, that jurists of reason would find it debatable whether the petition states a valid claim of the denial of a constitutional right.”
• noting that “Lindh requires a court of appeals to apply pre-AEDPA law in reviewing the trial court’s ruling, for cases commenced there pre-AEDPA”
• treating a notice of appeal as an application for a certificate of appealability
• "To obtain a COA under § 2253(c), a habeas prisoner must make a substantial showing of the denial of a constitutional right"
• holding that when initial habeas petition is dismissed for failure to exhaust state remedies, and not based on adjudication of the merits, subsequent habeas petition is not successive
• holding the post-AEDPA version of 28 U.S.C. § 2253 controls petitioner’s right to appeal denial of habeas relief when appeal is filed after effective date of AEDPA
• holding that the unnecessary misconduct of the prosecutor” as a concern requirements of § 2253(c
• “Where the public holds an exaggerated opinion of the accuracy of scientific testimony, the prejudice is likely to be indelible.”
• “[A] COA should issue when the prisoner shows, at least, that jurists of reason would find it debatable whether the petition states a valid claim of the denial of a constitutional right . . . .”
• “Where a district court has rejected the constitutional claims on the merits, the showing required to satisfy § 2253(c
• applying AEDPA, habeas petition filed after initial petition was dismissed for failure to exhaust state remedies is not a "second or successive petition."
• “A habeas petition filed in the district court after an initial habeas petition was unadjudicated on its merits and dismissed for failure to exhaust state remedies is not a second or successive petition.”
• “[E]ach step is part of a threshold inquiry, which must be satisfied before the court of appeals hears the appeal.” (internal quotation marks omitted)
• explaining that the phrase “second or successive,” as used in AEDPA, is a term of art
• “Except for substituting the word ‘constitutional’ for the word ‘federal,’ § 2253 is a codification of the [certificate of probable cause] standard.”
• requiring appellants to show that reasonable jurists could debate whether the petition should have been resolved differently or that the issues presented deserved encouragement to proceed further before granting a COA
• granting a COA signifies that the issues raised "`deserve encouragement to proceed further'"
• dismissal without prejudice under Lundy "contemplated that the prisoner could return to federal court after the requisite exhaustion"
• COA needed for claims decided on the merits and for claims dismissed on procedural grounds
